notes.1a: (i) Most candidates were able to complete the table to show the number of electrons in the 3p subshells of P, S and Cl, as 3, 4 and 5 respectively. The total number of unpaired electrons in these elements proved challenging for some candidates, Common incorrect answers were 1, 0 and 1 respectively.
notes.1aii: The equation to represent the first ionisation of P was well answered. A common error was to omit the state symbols of (g) throughout.
notes.1ii: The question required candidates to choose one of three possible values, given in the question, to represent the first ionisation energy of S and to explain their choice. Most candidates did not mention that S has a pair of electrons in a 3p orbital, which experience spin-pair repulsion. This results in S having an ionisation energy value of 1000kJ mol–1, which is lower than both P and Cl. The explanation required candidates to recall that whilst S has a nuclear charge higher than P and lower than Cl, its nuclear attraction to the outer electrons is the lowest of these three elements. Many candidates chose a value between P and Cl and supported their choice with a incorrect statement that the ‘nuclear attraction to the outer electrons’ increased across the period.
notes.1b: (i) The full electronic configuration of the P3─ ion was well answered as: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6.
notes.1bii: The decrease in ionic radius from P3─ to S2─ and Cl─ was well answered. Many correct explanations included mention of an increased attraction of the outer electron to the nucleus resulting from an increased nuclear charge with each ionic species having the same shielding.
notes.1c: Observations were required for three tests carried out on separate samples of NaCl(aq). When Br (aq) is added to a sample no reaction occurs, and the colourless solution of NaCl(aq) turns orange (because of the added Br ). Most answers stated that the observation from the addition of concentrated H SO to NaCl(aq) is 2 4 misty/steamy fumes, not recognising that the NaCl is in aqueous solution (and not a solid). The solution remains colourless as there is no visible reaction. A white precipitate is formed when AgNO (aq) is added to NaCl(aq).
notes.1d: (i) This question provided information that the chemical behaviour of POCl is similar to that of PCl ; 3 5 POCl has a low melting and boiling points and reacts vigorously with water suggesting that the structure and bonding of POCl is simple covalent. A small number of candidates gave a good explanation for this information and appreciated that the ‘simple’ structure of POCl was related to weak intermolecular forces of attractions and that the ‘covalent’ nature of the compound is linked to the hydrolysis reaction with water.
notes.1dii: The equation for the reaction of POCl with water was generally quite well answered. Errors included an incorrect formula for H PO and/or incorrect ratio between the water molecules and 3 4 HCl product.
notes.1iii: Most candidates were awarded full marks for the dot-and-cross diagram. A common error was the use of a dative bond between the P and O atoms.
notes.1e: (i) Most candidates were awarded the first mark for the definition of the enthalpy change of formation, for stating ‘enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed’. However, very few correctly stated the second requirement that it is ‘from its elements in their standard states’. Many answers mentioned standard conditions which was not a requirement.
notes.1eii: The calculation of the bond energy of P=O (in PCl ), using ∆H and bond energy (O ) data, proved 3 f 2 challenging for most candidates. Use of incorrect energy cycles was the major problem and full marks were rarely awarded. A correct energy cycle is: 2PCl (g) + O (g) → 2POCl (g) 3 2 3 2(–289) 2(–592) 2P + 3Cl + O 2 2 ∆H = 2(–592) – 2(–289) = -606 kJmol-1 bonds broken bonds formed 6 P-Cl 6 P-Cl 1 O=O (496) 2 P=O 496 - 2P=O = -606 -2P=O = -1102 P=O = 551kJmol-1
notes.2a: (i) The solubilities of group 2 hydroxides ‘increases’ down the group; this variation in solubilities was correctly stated by many candidates
notes.2aii: When barium oxide is added to water the observation is that the white solid dissolves/disappears to form a colourless solution. A common error was that there was bubbling/effervescence seen.
notes.2iii: In the given reaction scheme, reaction 2 involved the formation of BaCO and water from adding a reactant to Ba(OH) . Carbon dioxide, CO , is a reactant that would form both the carbonate and 2 2 water. Many answers included a metal carbonate which would not give water as a product.
notes.2iv: The addition of ethanoic acid to Ba(OH) gave barium ethanoate, (CH COO) Ba, as the product. 2 3 2 Many candidates appreciated that barium ethanoate was formed but opted to answer using a formula of (CH COO)Ba, which was not creditworthy.
notes.2v: Ba(OH) and hydrogen are formed when Ba is added to water and the equation is: Ba + 2H O → Ba(OH) + H 2 2 2 A common error was to use only 1 mole of water molecules and water formed as a product.
notes.2b: (i) The thermal stability of group 2 carbonates increases down the group; hence, when barytocalcite, BaCa(CO ) , is heated CaCO will decompose first. Most answers correctly stated that CaCO 3 2 3 3 would decompose first but explanations compared the reactivity of Ca with Ba.
notes.2bii: The equation to represent the thermal decomposition of BaCa(CO ) was often correct. 3 2 BaCa(CO ) → BaO + CaO + 2CO 3 2 2 Common errors included answers with BaCa as a product or omitting 2CO as a product.
notes.2c: Full credit for the hydrolysis reaction was rarely awarded. The two organic products are methanol, CH OH, and the diacid. That both the –CN and –CO CH groups will undergo hydrolysis was not recognised by many 2 3 candidates. The –CN group was frequently left unhydrolysed and the product methanol was not given as the second organic product.
notes.3a: The definition of an oxidising agent, as a species that oxidises another species, and is reduced in the process by the gain of electrons, was overall generally well answered.
notes.3b: This question required the completion of an energy diagram/energy profile to represent the catalytic effect of MnO (s) on the decomposition of KClO (s). This entailed drawing two labelled curves 2 3 representing the uncatalysed and the catalysed profiles. Many answers were awarded full credit. Common errors included unlabelled diagrams or profiles with only one curve.
notes.3c: The term disproportionation is used to describe the oxidation and reduction of a single element, in the same chemical reaction. Here the reaction involved KClO being converted to KClO and KCl, 3 4 in which the Cl is both oxidised and reduced in this reaction. Many chose the correct element; there were, however, several answers that identified K or KClO as the species undergoing simultaneous redox.
notes.3d: (i) PV=nRT was successfully used by many candidates to calculate the volume of 1 mole of gas, in a reaction of glucose with molten KClO , to give the correct answer of 0.0524m3, to 3 significant figures. 4KCl O + C H O → 6CO + 6H O + 4KCl 3 6 12 6 2 2 Several candidates did not appear to read the question carefully and gave answers with an incorrect number of sig. figs and/or incorrect rounding of their answers.
notes.3dii: This question required the calculation of the moles of glucose, (5/180) and to use this value, together with their answer from 3(d)(i), to calculate total volume of the gaseous CO and H O in the 2 2 equation. Many candidates were able to correctly calculate the moles of glucose but then failed to multiply this value by 12 to determine the total moles of CO and H O produced. 2 2 Several answers then continued to repeat the calculation in 3(d)(i) instead of using their answer from 3(d)(i).
notes.3e: (i) A high proportion of candidates correctly identified the number of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohol groups, in glucose, as 1, 4 and zero, respectively.
notes.3eii: This question required observations for three tests. The observation for a reaction of glucose + warm, acidified KMnO (aq) is that the solution changes from purple to colourless. Many candidates were given credit for a correct observation. Glucose + warm, Fehling’s reagent gave an orange/red precipitate which again was recognised by many candidates. Several candidates omitted the precipitate or stated that a silver mirror formed. Glucose + warm, alkaline I (aq) was incorrectly stated as a yellow precipitate by many candidates. There is no reaction with glucose, so the solution remains colourless.
notes.3iii: Several candidates were able to correctly define structural isomers as ‘molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae’.
notes.4a: (i) Most candidates correctly gave the systematic name of the alkene D, with a molecular formula of C H , as 3-methylbut-1-ene. 5 10
notes.4aii: Few candidates gave a correct explanation of why the alkenes, C and D, did not exhibit geometric isomerism. In C, one C (in the C=C bond) has two methyl groups and in D, one C (in the C=C) has two hydrogen atoms; neither will exhibit geometrical isomerism.
notes.4iii: This question required an explanation as to why different major products were formed when HBr reacts separately with C and D. Many candidates appreciated that methyl/alkyl groups are responsible for a positive inductive effect and that the more alkyl groups, surrounding the carbocation, the more stable is the carbocation intermediate. However, the application of this concept to the intermediates of C and D was not well recognised. 9701 Chemistry November 2023 Common errors were statements that the tertiary halogenoalkane was more stable, in C, and the secondary halogenoalkane was more stable, in D, rather than their respective intermediate carbocations. Many candidates quoted Markovnikov’s rule without any further explanation.
notes.4iv: When D is reacted with H (g), 2-methylbutane, CH CH(CH )CH CH , is formed. Many candidates 2 3 3 2 3 omitted the brackets surrounding the side-chain methyl group, on the CH group.
notes.4v: Many candidates gave a monomer containing only two methyl groups or structures that still contained a double bond.
notes.4b: The question contained information regarding the relative intensities of the M and (M + 1) ions, from a mass spectrum of C, which showed a molecular ion peak at 70. Many candidates correctly calculated that C contained 5C atoms but then failed to use this information, in conjunction with the molecular ion peak, 70, to confirm that the molecular formula of C was C H . 5 10
notes.4c: (i) The mechanism for the addition of HBr to C, 2-methylbut-2-ene, was quite well answered. Common errors included full charges on the H-Br, instead of a dipole, curly arrows, from C=C to Hδ+ of HBr, arrows starting at one end of the C=C bond and intermediates with both a –ve charge and a partial negative charge.
notes.4cii: This question was well answered with a common error being the use of C H , instead of the 3 7 unambiguous expanded version, (CH ) CH–. 3 2
notes.4d: Please note that due to an issue with diagram labelling in this question, full marks have been awarded to all candidates to make sure that no candidates were disadvantaged. This has been corrected in the published version of the paper. The question required completion of a table of reagents and conditions for a reaction scheme. The formation of alcohol, F, from a halogenoalkane, E, required the use of NaOH(aq). Cleavage of the double bond, in C, to form a carboxylic acid, G, and propanone, was carried out using hot acidified concentrated KMnO . The formation of ester, H, from F and G, needed concentrated H SO (as a catalyst). 2 4
notes.general_comments:
Definitions and basic concepts of chemistry are still causing candidates difficulties, particularly with enthalpy
and isomerism topics. Definitions should explain accurately what the term means.
The use of brackets to surround side-chain groups, should be encouraged, when writing structural formulae.
